procedural_history.impugned_order: Common judgment of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Bench at Jabalpur dated 12th October, 2022, in Criminal Appeal No. 10474 of 2019 and Criminal Appeal No. 10549 of 2019.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court dismissed Criminal Appeal No. 10474 of 2019 filed by Manoj Kumar Soni, who challenged his conviction under Section 411 IPC, and Criminal Appeal No. 10549 of 2019 filed by Kallu @ Habib, who challenged his conviction under Section 120-B IPC. These appeals were filed under Section 374(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Manoj and Kallu filed Special Leave Petitions (SLPs) before the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment. The SLPs of three other accused (Suleman, Arif, and Jaihind) were dismissed. Notice was issued on the SLPs of Manoj and Kallu on 06th April, 2023 and 11th April, 2023, respectively. The Supreme Court is hearing the appeals by special leave.

directions: Manoj and Kallu are acquitted and set free.
Manoj and Kallu shall be immediately released from custody, if not wanted in any other case.

issue.issue_text: Whether a conviction based largely upon disclosure statements, unaccompanied by supporting evidence, is justified.

facts: The appellants' convictions for offenses under sections 411 and 120-B of the IPC were based largely on disclosure statements made by them and a co-accused.
The sole connecting evidence against the appellants was the recovery of items based on these disclosure statements.
There was no other significant supporting evidence presented by the prosecution to corroborate the statements.
law: Disclosure statements, while significant as a contributing factor, are not strong enough on their own to prove charges beyond a reasonable doubt.
Under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, 1872, information from an accused leading to a discovery is just one link in the chain of proof; other links must be established by law.

Courts have consistently hesitated to rely solely on the disclosure statements of a co-accused. Such statements are typically used only to support or "lend assurance to" other independent evidence against an accused.
application: The Court found it implausible that disclosure statements alone could be adequate to secure a conviction.

It determined that the recovery based on the appellants' statements was not sufficient to qualify as a "fact … discovered" within the meaning of Section 27 of the Evidence Act, and was therefore untrustworthy.
Since the prosecution's entire case was premised on these disclosure statements without any other satisfactory evidence, the statements could not be used to sustain the conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a conviction based largely upon disclosure statements, unaccompanied by supporting evidence, is not justified. The Court held that such statements are not sufficient on their own to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Consequently, the appellants' convictions were set aside, and they were acquitted.

issue.issue_text: Whether seizure evidence can be considered reliable when the seizure witnesses have turned hostile.

facts: All four independent witnesses (PW-5, PW-6, PW-11, and PW-16) who were supposed to corroborate the seizure of property turned hostile.
These witnesses testified that they did not witness the seizure but were made to sign the seizure memos by the police ('daroga'), with some signing at the police station.
This created significant contradictions between the testimony of the police witnesses and the independent seizure witnesses.
The trial court had relied on the police witnesses' statements while overlooking the testimony of the hostile independent witnesses.
law: While corroboration of police testimony by independent witnesses is not always mandatory, if the prosecution presents such witnesses and they turn hostile, the court must evaluate their testimony.
If hostile witnesses create a "gaping hole" in the prosecution's theory about the search and seizure, the case can collapse.

The standalone testimony of police officers regarding a seizure is not considered convincing or conclusive when all independent witnesses presented by the prosecution turn hostile and contradict the police account.
application: The Court found that the seizure lost all credibility because every single independent witness turned hostile.
The witnesses provided a consistent version of events: they were coerced into signing the seizure memos by the police, which directly undermined the legitimacy of the seizure process.
The Court stated that it could not selectively rely on parts of the hostile witnesses' depositions; their testimony as a whole discredited the seizure.

The Court described the testimony of the seizure witnesses as the "only thread" that could have tied the case together. Since they all turned hostile, the Court concluded that the seizure itself was "falsified."
Consequently, the Court held that the uncorroborated testimony of the Investigating Officer regarding the seizure was insufficient and had to be rejected.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the seizure evidence as unreliable. It reasoned that because all the independent witnesses to the seizure turned hostile and testified that they were made to sign the seizure documents by the police, the entire seizure process lost its credibility, and the standalone testimony of the police witnesses was not sufficient to prove it.

issue.issue_text: Whether a presumption of fact under Section 114(a) of the Evidence Act can be drawn in isolation, without corroboration from other cogent evidence, to convict an accused.

facts: The Trial Court convicted an accused ('M'), a goldsmith, for possessing stolen property under Section 411, IPC.
The conviction was based on a presumption under Section 114(a) of the Evidence Act, which was drawn because stolen articles were allegedly recovered from his possession shortly after a theft.
The primary evidence against 'M' was the recovery of these articles based on disclosure statements made by him and other co-accused.
law: Section 114(a) of the Evidence Act allows a court to presume that a person in possession of stolen goods soon after a theft is either the thief or has knowingly received stolen property.

This presumption is not absolute. Its application depends on various factors, including the nature of the stolen items, the circumstances of recovery, the time lapse, and the explanation provided by the accused.
Disclosure statements, while a contributing factor, are not strong enough on their own to prove charges beyond a reasonable doubt.
application: The Supreme Court ruled that a presumption of fact under Section 114(a) cannot be drawn in isolation; it must be supported by other cogent, corroborating evidence.
The Court found that the Trial Court erred by convicting 'M' solely on this presumption without considering other critical factors.
The Court identified several weaknesses in the prosecution's case that made the presumption unreliable:
1. The evidence, consisting mainly of disclosure statements, was insufficient for a conviction.
2. The accused's profession as a goldsmith provided a reasonable context for him to be in possession of a significant quantity of ornaments, which weakened the presumption of guilt.

3. There were "serious procedural lapses" in the identification process of the recovered articles, which meant the prosecution failed to conclusively prove that the items found with 'M' were the ones stolen from the complainant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that a presumption under Section 114(a) can be used in isolation to secure a conviction. The Court held that such a presumption must be drawn in consideration of all other evidence on record and requires corroboration. Because the supporting evidence against the accused was weak and the Trial Court failed to consider relevant factors, the presumption was wrongly applied, and the conviction was set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a conviction based largely upon disclosure statements, unaccompanied by supporting evidence, is justified.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, as framed by the issue, is that a conviction is not justified if it is based primarily on disclosure statements that are not supported by other corroborating evidence.
respondent_arguments: The respondent/State argued that the Trial Court and High Court had carefully and meticulously considered all materials and evidence on record and arrived at a just conclusion, which should not be interfered with.

arguments.issue_text: Whether seizure evidence can be considered reliable when the seizure witnesses have turned hostile.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, as framed by the issue, is that evidence related to a seizure cannot be considered reliable if the witnesses to that seizure have turned hostile (i.e., did not support the prosecution's case in their testimony).
respondent_arguments: The respondent/State argued that the lower courts had delved deep into the materials, found no material contradiction in the testimonies, and that any procedural flaws pointed out by the appellant did not result in a failure of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a presumption of fact under Section 114(a) of the Evidence Act can be drawn in isolation, without corroboration from other cogent evidence, to convict an accused.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, as framed by the issue, is that a legal presumption under Section 114(a) of the Evidence Act is not sufficient on its own to convict an accused; it must be supported by other strong, corroborating evidence.
respondent_arguments: The respondent/State supported the lower courts' judgments, submitting that they were based on a careful consideration of all materials on record and that the appellant had not established a sufficient case for the Supreme Court to interfere.

cases.principle: A presumption of fact under Section 114(a) of the Evidence Act must be drawn considering other evidence on record and must not be drawn in isolation without corroboration from other cogent evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where two persons are indicted for conspiring together and are tried together, both must be acquitted, or both must be convicted.
obiter: The law on the evidentiary value of disclosure statements of a co-accused is settled; courts hesitate to place sole reliance on such statements.

The Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, having regard to the common course of natural events, human conduct, and public and private business, in their relation to the facts of the particular case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the convictions were unsustainable and appeared "far-fetched" because they were not based on credible, supporting evidence but rather on "illusory knowledge." The conviction for conspiracy against one appellant was found to be based on wholly insufficient grounds, namely a minor monetary recovery and a past employment connection. Furthermore, the Trial Court erred by drawing a presumption of fact without considering other necessary factors and by overlooking significant contradictions between the testimonies of police witnesses and independent seizure witnesses who had turned hostile.
legal_tests_applied: In a conspiracy charge where two or more persons are named, if all but one are acquitted, a valid judgment of conviction cannot be passed upon the one remaining person. (Topandas vs. State of Bombay)
A presumption of fact cannot be drawn in isolation without the court considering other corroborating factors. (A Devendran vs. State of Tamil Nadu)
